doc.title: Eric Alexander interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Would Eric be a valid example for a young jazz aspirant
summary: Alexander says he started late, knowing two tunes at 18-19, and advises young people to commit five or six years while they have time to recover.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I have a little scenario I was going to start off with. Let’s suppose my son or daughter is about 19, which has now passed, but they are an avid jazz musician, quite passionate, and they’re looking at a career in jazz, and I say to them, “That’s an awful tough life with not much security,” etc. etc. And they answer to me, “Yeah, but look at Eric Alexander.” Is that a —
A valid response to my parental concern?

Well if they knew a lot about me it might be semi-valid because, you know, if they were to say look, Eric Alexander, when he was 18 or 19 years old, knew about two tunes by heart, couldn’t improvise through a jazz blues effectively, didn’t know the changes to that, and he told his parents the same thing and they said you’re crazy, you know, stick a fork in that idea. But he figured out how to play in a very short period of time and ended up having a relatively successful career. You know if they knew all that information I would say well it’s actually not such a bad answer. I think if I were a parent, and I wasn’t who I am but I had some understanding of the situation, I think what I would tell my kids is there’s no time like the present. If you really want to give this a shot, do it while you’re young. You know, devote five or six years of your life to pursuing this dream as best you can with every ounce of effort you have and every bit of love you have for the music. See where that takes you. If you get to a point where it becomes painfully, for sure, but painfully apparent that you just aren’t going to be able to do it, you’ll have time to turn around and do something else. But don’t let a really deep-seated love for the music fester inside your body until you are a middle-aged person and then suddenly freak out and tell your wife or husband oh my God I’ve been living a lie my whole life, I have to pursue my dream of jazz. I’m quitting my job and I’ll try to support the kids as best I can. I mean I’ve seen that happen to people. And I think that’s really a far scarier scenario than a late-
teen person, you know, with a certain amount of musical talent thinking, yeah I want to give this a try. I think it’s okay to try things when you’re young, because you have time to recover.
